title: Orion Systems POC Traffic Signature Kickoff
summary: Initial POC scoping to capture Orion's QPS/concurrency profile, token distributions, success criteria, and timeline. Agreed to run a 2-week bench with Redwood hosted endpoints and a follow-up dedicated capacity estimate. Security docs requested; benchmark template and data sample to be shared.
next_steps: Marco to send POC benchmark template and tokens distribution spreadsheet by 2025-07-02
Priya to share a 48-hour sample of request logs (anonymized) by 2025-07-03
Lena to schedule a dedicated-capacity estimate session the week of 2025-07-07
Jasmine to share SOC2 summary and VPC design doc link within 48h
action_items: Priya Desai — export and sanitize 48h request logs (due 2025-07-03)
Lena Park — prepare dedicated capacity estimate + cost ballpark (due 2025-07-09)
Jasmine O'Neill — attach SOC2 and encryption/KMS notes (due 2025-06-29)
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-27 15:00 PDT | Duration: 00:48:00 | Attendees: Lena Park, Marco Ruiz, Jasmine O'Neill (Redwood); Priya Desai, Tomás Alvarez, Rachel Kim, Evan Holt (Orion)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll get into the traffic signature and success criteria for the POC.
[00:12] Priya Desai: Hi, Priya here. We're excited to scope this out.
[00:15] Tomás Alvarez: Tomás, platform. We just want to make sure latency and cost lines up with our SLA.
[00:22] Rachel Kim: Rachel on the call as well.
[00:24] Lena Park: Awesome. Marco, do you want to kick off on what we typically capture for the workload profile?
[00:30] Marco Ruiz: Sure. Hi all, Marco from Redwood infra. So the POC we're proposing is two-fold: an ingestion-phase check to validate correctness and a performance-phase to run controlled QPS/concurrency patterns that reflect your production mix. We'll need QPS peak, median, concurrency, average input token length and output token length distributions. If you have percentiles for sequence length that helps.
[00:55] Priya Desai: We have rough numbers. Right now our front end hits our service at around 120 qps average, with spikes to 1.2k during batch events — those are rare. Median concurrency per model worker is about 14. Prompt sizes: avg input ~ 80 tokens, output ~ 220 tokens but with a long tail.
[01:15] Marco Ruiz: Got it. That long tail is important for KV cache sizing and tail latency. Do you have a token distribution histogram or p95/p99 lengths?
[01:25] Priya Desai: We can pull p50/p95/p99. I think p95 output is about 600 tokens, p99 around 1.6k but again that's very rare.
[01:33] Evan Holt: Those long ones are usually internal agent conversations, not user-facing. We can probably exclude some of them from the primary SLA.
[01:40] Marco Ruiz: Good note. For the POC we usually model three profiles: main web traffic (short prompts), session-based agents (medium with some caching), and long-form generator jobs. We'll simulate a 72-hour run with a mix: 85% web-short, 12% session medium, 3% long-form.
[02:00] Lena Park: That split sounds reasonable. Timeline-wise we propose: 1) baseline functional validation (2 days), 2) run the 72-hour mixed workload and collect token-level latency/cost (7 days counting analysis), then 3) dedicated capacity estimate and optional canary.
[02:18] Rachel Kim: How much of this can be run on Redwood hosted vs dedicated? Security is a big ask for us — we need VPC and KMS.
[02:26] Marco Ruiz: For the initial bench we recommend Redwood hosted endpoints (fast onboarding) with TLS in transit and option for encrypted-at-rest. We can run a private, VPC-attached endpoint for a follow-up stage. KMS integrations and customer-managed keys are part of the Private offering, but we can provide SOC2 docs now.
[02:43] Jasmine O'Neill: I'll share the SOC2 and a high-level VPC design doc after this call.
[02:48] Tomás Alvarez: For the benchmarking we need to understand burst capacity and autoscaling behavior — how do you emulate token mix impact on throughput?
[02:56] Marco Ruiz: Two levers: request-level concurrency and batch size. Token mix affects per-token compute — so throughput in tokens/sec changes with longer outputs. Our benchmark harness instruments tokens-per-second, GPU utlil — uh util, and end-to-end tail latencies. We'll also capture model variant fallbacks if we trigger any cost-optimized paths.
[03:18] Priya Desai: Do you support prefix/KV cache across sessions? We have a lot of session re-use.
[03:24] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we have session-aware KV caching. For the POC we can enable KV cache and measure hit rates; you'll want to provide a realistic session-id distribution. If you don't have that, we can approximate with sticky-session simulation.
[03:36] Rachel Kim: On success criteria — what do you recommend we measure?
[03:40] Marco Ruiz: Typical success criteria: p95 latency under 350ms for web-short, cost per 1k tokens below your threshold, and no unrecoverable errors at your peak QPS for X hours (we'll define X). Also monitoring of token-level cost breakdown and autoscaler stability.
[03:56] Priya Desai: Our internal goal is p95 < 400ms for interactive flows and cost target of $Y per 1k tokens — I'll put the dollar numbers in the spreadsheet.
[04:06] Lena Park: Great. Can you confirm the peak qps numbers including concurrent in-flight requests?
[04:10] Priya Desai: Peak observed 1.2k qps for 10 minutes during our nightly batch kickoff. Sustained peak for business hours is about 350 qps. Concurrency tends to go to 220 concurrent in-flight across our pool during peaks.
[04:23] Marco Ruiz: Ok we will simulate both sustained and spike patterns. For sustained 350 qps we may instrument steady-state runs to observe thermal behavior and cache hit stabilization. For spikes we'll do a 10-min ramp.
[04:36] Tomás Alvarez: Regarding model selection: we use a mid-sized open model for most cases, occasionally running a larger finetuned variant for high-quality responses. How will you handle model fallbacks?
[04:48] Marco Ruiz: We'll configure routing to fallback to a quantized variant if we hit capacity limits; we'll also measure quality delta using your eval prompts if you provide them. For latency-sensitive flows we can pin to a faster variant and for background jobs allow cheaper variants.
[05:02] Rachel Kim: Can we also capture costs for burst vs reserved capacity? We need to justify a dedicated pool.
[05:08] Marco Ruiz: Absolutely — the bench will include cost modeling for hosted per-token pricing vs Dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commit amortized across observed throughput). We'll produce a cost-per-1M tokens estimate under your mix.
[05:21] Priya Desai: About data residency — some customers require EU-only. We're currently global but we want to test EU region performance for a subset.
[05:30] Marco Ruiz: Noted. We can run region-targeted benches; that will help us identify cross-region latencies. If you need private control plane for EU, that's part of Redwood Private.
[05:39] Evan Holt: For the logs — we need audit trails and token-level traceability. How granular is logging during the POC?
[05:45] Marco Ruiz: We emit per-request traces: timestamp, model, prompt hash (we can hash prompts for privacy), input/output token counts, latency, and GPU host telemetry. Full request bodies are optional and only with agreement; otherwise hashed or redacted.
[06:01] Priya Desai: We'll probably want hashed prompts and token counts. We'll send a sanitized example.
[06:05] Lena Park: Great. Let's walk through the benchmark template at a high level — Marco?
[06:10] Marco Ruiz: Template: workload mix, token length distributions (p50/p95/p99), request rate schedule (steady + spikes), concurrency targets, session reuse pattern, model variants, and success criteria. We'll instrument metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, GPU util, cost per request. We also capture error types.
[06:34] Tomás Alvarez: One nuance: some requests are multi-step tool calls — like a retrieval call then a generation. Those show up as two requests; do you model multi-hop flows?
[06:44] Marco Ruiz: We can model multi-step flows; we recommend combining them in the harness as a single scenario with internal think-time. That way we can represent end-to-end latency and per-step token accounting.
[06:57] Priya Desai: About the long tail — if p99 is 1.6k tokens we need to budget for outliers in the dedicated capacity.
[07:05] Marco Ruiz: Correct. That's why we provide two capacity views: 99th-percentile dimensioned capacity and a cost-optimized view that leans on fallback variants for the tail.
[07:15] Lena Park: Quick question on metrics: do you have built-in tooling to map tokens to GPU cycles per variant so we can project cost?
[07:23] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we have calibrated per-model tokens-to-gpu-ms baselines across hardware families. For the POC we'll run an initial microbenchmark to calibrate to your model and hardware and then extrapolate for the 72-hour run.
[07:39] Rachel Kim: What's the POC acceptance criteria operationally? Do we require 2 weeks of no-regressions?
[07:46] Marco Ruiz: Our typical acceptance is: reproducible workload run, meet defined latency & error SLOs during a sustained window (e.g., 6 hours), and cost within X% of estimate. We can make that explicit in the SOW.
[07:58] Priya Desai: Can you quantify X%? We want to be conservative.
[08:02] Lena Park: Usually customers pick 10–20% variance tolerance; we'll propose 15% in the draft SOW unless you want a tighter bound.
[08:09] Priya Desai: 15% is fine to start.
[08:13] Tomás Alvarez: Networking — do you need us to open special egress, or will the hosted endpoints initiate connections?
[08:18] Marco Ruiz: Hosted endpoints are standard TLS endpoints; no special egress. For VPC/private deployments we'll coordinate ingress rules and peering — Jasmine will follow up with the VPC design template.
[08:30] Jasmine O'Neill: I'll attach the network checklist after this call.
[08:33] Evan Holt: For the 72-hour run, how do you seed data for cache hits to stabilize before measurement window?
[08:40] Marco Ruiz: We recommend a warm-up phase — 2–4 hours of scaled traffic before the measurement window to allow KV caching and batch pipelines to warm. We'll define the warm-up pattern in the template.
[08:52] Priya Desai: About measurement windows: we want p95 and p99 during business hours and a separate analysis for off-peak.
[08:58] Marco Ruiz: We'll split the analysis windows accordingly and provide per-window breakdowns.
[09:04] Lena Park: Let's talk practicalities: samples we need from you: a 48-hour anonymized log extract, typical session-id distribution, and a short eval set for quality comparisons.
[09:15] Priya Desai: We'll aim to provide those by early next week.
[09:20] Marco Ruiz: Great. On the Redwood side we'll return the benchmark template and a script to replay logs in our harness. We'll also provide a cost projection and a recommended Dedicated pool size if you want to compare.
[09:34] Rachel Kim: For model ops, can we pin model versions for the POC so devs can reproduce results?
[09:39] Marco Ruiz: Yes we pin versions and record hashes. We also snapshot runtime config including quantization level.
[09:45] Tomás Alvarez: Any gotchas we should expect in throttling or queuing behavior during spikes?
[09:50] Marco Ruiz: Two things: queueing increases latency non-linearly under heavy load, and batching can create tail amplification for long prompts. We'll surface these in the report and propose policies (max concurrent per-client, request timeouts) to bound user-facing latency.
[10:04] Priya Desai: Can you simulate an outage fallback — like degraded to cheaper variant — to confirm graceful degradation?
[10:09] Marco Ruiz: Yes, that's part of our chaos scenarios: simulate a pool constraint and route a fraction to fallback model; measure quality and latency impact.
[10:18] Rachel Kim: On instrumentation — will you provide per-route dashboards?
[10:21] Marco Ruiz: Yes, Redwood Console will show per-route token breakdowns, cost, p95/p99 latency, and autoscaler events. We can give you a demo link post-POC.
[10:34] Lena Park: Alright, let's capture next steps and owners. Marco, you send the template. Priya will send logs. Jasmine will share SOC2 and network checklist. Lena will coordinate the dedicated estimate.
[10:46] Priya Desai: Quick question — is there a limit on concurrent sessions we can simulate in the harness? We might want to go beyond 1k to test stress.
[10:53] Marco Ruiz: We can simulate higher concurrency; for hosted runs we'll be mindful of fair-use and may throttle noisy tests. For stress tests we often recommend a short dedicated trial run.
[11:05] Tomás Alvarez: For the billing model during the POC, is it usage-based?
[11:09] Lena Park: Yes, initial POC is usage-based. We'll provide an estimate and you can optionally sign up for a short dedicated reservation if you want to run heavy stress tests.
[11:18] Rachel Kim: Ok. Any regulatory questions? We will need an audit trail for the POC.
[11:22] Jasmine O'Neill: We'll include audit logs and explain retention options; default is 30 days unless you need longer.
[11:28] Priya Desai: Great. When should we sync next?
[11:30] Lena Park: After Marco sends the template and you send logs, let's meet the week of 2025-07-07 to finalize the schedule. I'll send a Doodle after this call.
[11:38] Marco Ruiz: One last technical note — when you share the logs, please include a small sample of the multi-step flows so we can model them correctly.
[11:47] Priya Desai: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[11:50] Rachel Kim: Thanks.
[11:52] Lena Park: Thanks, meeting adjourned.

Meeting recap (auto-generated): 48-minute scoping call covering workload profile and POC plan. Agreed 72-hour mixed workload bench with warm-up phase, success criteria (p95 latency, cost target, error SLOs), and follow-up dedicated capacity estimate. Action items and next steps recorded above.

Notes on transcription quality: some technical terms may be mis-transcribed (KV cache -> KV cash, quantization -> quantize-ation) and punctuation may be off.
